doc.title: Mandel Johnny — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

chapter: Gil Evans, Birth of the Cool and the Second Herd
title: Blossom Dearie brings him to Gil Evans
summary: Mandel lived a block from Gil Evans without knowing it until Blossom Dearie told him to meet Gil; he recalls knowing Mulligan and the Georgie Auld small band.

story.theme_name: Playing with and around Miles Davis
story.community_name: Playing with Miles Davis: joining, sessions and the band

blocks.x: So how did you get involved with Gil and that whole circle of people?
Oh, strangely enough the first person to bring me around, I lived right on the other side of the block of Gil and I didn’t know they were all there and I didn’t know Gil or anything.

Yeah and I lived on 54th and I didn’t know it, I was still living with my mother at the time and… Blossom Dearie who I had been in Alvino Rey’s group with, she came in as the lead singer. She had been with Woody before that and I just didn’t believe her.
I can’t imagine her as a band singer.
She was, she was the lead singer in the group the, Blue Reys.
Really? With that tiny little voice?
It was a wonderful pure voice.
She was seventeen years old for God sakes, looked like a milkmaid.

A little Norwegian milkmaid from upstate New York. She came out full blown, she could play the piano, she could sing, she had a very – her pitch was so great, that she was wonderful on top of the group. And yeah, that’s what she was doing first.
So she introduced you to Gil?
She told me about Gil Evans, oh you gotta meet Gil Evans, I said, “great,” and I fell in love with Gil immediately.
You’d heard the stuff he had written for, Thornhill then?

I had, but not a whole lot. I loved Thornhill’s band and I guess there was more Gil then I knew. Then I got to know Gil and Gerry and I had been hanging around since 1945, I met him when he was still with Krupa and had written, “Disc Jockey Jump.” We were with Georgie Auld’s small band together for a while in ‘47. There were a lot of bands interspersed in there, Georgie Auld for a while didn’t have a big band, he had a small band with Serge Chaloff and with Gerry and… I can’t remember everybody, it was like a nine piece band sort of like the Tentet. We were all experimenting with smaller instrumentations because people were finding it easier to get work with smaller groups than the standard big sized one. From about ‘47 on and… that’s right it was sort of also a forerunner of what became the cool sound, you know there’d be one trumpet, one trombone, three saxophone bands, you’d have a five or six man frontline.
